Color Images: The "Tender" Books We have noted that in the four books of the "tender" series , narrative segments are shorter. The narrator is less expansive than in the "tough" books . At the same time , color images grow in importance and power, evolving from their ancillary, almost incidental role in the "tough" series, towards a new , generative one. Color words dominate the scenes in which they occur, extending their aura over the entire textual segment, and bearing with it the emotional tonalities occasioned by the events being described. As the narrator comes closer to recounting his earliest recollections, these incandescent color words assume even greater power. In Pays sans chapeau, the "tender" novel that depicts the most recent events in the narrator's life, he returns to Haiti after a long absence. As we have seen, the mature author is overcome by the sensual richness of this Caribbean environment and affirms the "primitive" character of his art. The sensations that rain down upon him include heat, odors , sounds, and of course colors evoked in such details as "feuilles jaunes," \[yellow leaves\] "les mouches tantot noires, tantot bleues" \[flies sometimes black, sometimes blue\] (34), and a cup of black coffee poured out in libation to the ancestors. The importance of this heightened sensual awareness is emphasized later in the book when the narrator returns from Ginen, the land of the dead. When he protests to the ethnologist Jean-Baptiste Romain that he is disappointed with what he has seen, the profes sor replies: "\[Lja-bas , au moins, ca vit, les sentiments sont pousses it l'extreme \[. ..\], les couleurs sont aussi tres vives (Ie noir, Ie rouge , Ie violet et Ie blanc etincelant)" \[Down there , at least, there is life, feelings are pushed to extremes \[...\], colors are also very powerful (black, red, violet, and sparkling white)\] (217). Colors brighten and sensations intensify in this special land of dreamlike experience. Such heightened acuity persists throughout the book . A poor woman wants to give him her beautiful daughter, dressed, predictably, in yellow (72) . Elsewhere, when he encounters a girlfriend of earlier days, he recalls the moment long past when he looked upon her with different eyes: "A un moment donne , je me suis retourne et je l'ai vue. Comme je ne l'avais jamais vue auparavant. Comme je ne verrai jamais plus une femme. Elle etait lit dans cette robe jaune. On etait en avril. Tout etait parfait" \[At one moment I turned and saw her. As I had never seen her before. As I will never see any other woman. She was

Dany Laferriere, "Primitive" Writer

there in that yellow dress. It was April. Everything was perfect\] (190I). Again, yellow combines sensual awareness with surprise, renewed vision, sharp realization, epiphany . Chronique de fa derive douce is a book very different from Pays sans chapeau, thematically , stylistically, and typographically . The narrative segments are very short (0.34 pages on average), grouped in six sections of unequal length corresponding to the unrolling of the seasons. Some sections consist of short poems in free verse, while others appear as longer continuous paragraphs. As has been noted, the book deals with the narrator' s first year in exile in Montreal. Much surprises the narrator, from the moment of arrival. It is a time of discovery and realization. Although the themes of racial difference and rivalry are present, they are downplayed. The narrator does not yet possess the cocky self-confidence of Comment faire I'amour, the book he prepares to write as he sets himself up in the park at the end of Chronique de fa derive douce. Stylistically, color words are used in a manner that has not been seen in the other books of the Autobiographie examined up to this point. In the poetic, whimsical, impressionistic segments of Chronique de fa derive douce, color images, often incisively reinforced by a color word inserted at the end of the segment, play a pivotal role in the development of the thought in the segment. They literally color the whole section, a flash of light illuminating an otherwise darkened scene. This important characteristic is shared, as will be shown, with both L 'odeur du cafe and Le charme des apres-midi sans fin . At the beginning of the book, the narrator steps from the aircraft and is immediately struck by the sight of a couple kissing in public, a cultural difference charged with sensual power, punctuated by the perception of a highly visible and suggestive color: "Un couple en train! de s'embrasser/ it l'aeroport.z Un baiser interminable '! La fille est en! minijupe rouge" \[a couple/ kissing / in the airport/ An endless kiss/ The girl is in/ a red miniskirt\] (11). The following segment culminates in the same color word "rouge," but this time the color is transferred from the miniskirt to the kiss itself (perhaps in association with red lips): "Je suis seul it m'interesser/ it ce baiser rouge" \[I alone am interested! in this red kiss\] (12). Red has been seen to symbolize the enduring heat of passion rather than the flash and surprise of coup de foudre . Since the narrator discovers here the relative freedom enjoyed

by these lovers in North America, red seems to be the appropriate color. After an initial period of disorientation and bewilderment in which color images are absent (12-39), the narrator quickly regains a sense of equilibrium, and adopts a more interactive attitude. He moves to new lodgings, expands his circle of acquaintances, meets attractive young White women, and begins his more aggressive exploration of the city and society. When he looks for a new apartment, the sign on the lawn is red (43). Once inside, he notes the walls are yellow (44). He notices a girl and follows her into a park. She wears "une courte robe jaune" \[a short yellow dress\] (57), as does in a later scene his boss's secretary (91). The sun glows red on this occasion (94), and the secretary (whose neck turns red when she hears the boss joking about sex \[79\]), gives him a red scarf as protection against the oncoming cold (109). When the boss's blond daughter arrives on the scene, the narrator notes her red lips (115); she leaves with his Indigenous colleague in a red convertible . When summer returns, another young woman in a red miniskirt passionately kisses her companion in public. The narrator cannot bear the tension created: "Je passe sans m'arreter" \[I walk by without stopping\] (129). He is attracted to his young female neighbor, who wears a yellow dress (124). However, she turns out to be lesbian; her passions are reserved for another. While yellow and red dominate these multiple, repetitive scenes of observation, desire, discovery, and involvement, the colors associated with the narrator's other lovers complete the spectrum . Nathalie, whom he loves for sex (84), wears a black dress (76), while Julie, "si serieuse" (133), dresses in cool blue (133). The generous and practical fat woman from the laundry is characterized by white (skin \[51\], sheets \[52\]). Green is present here only in the description of the tree the narrator sees outside his apartment window (71). The lush greens of Haiti are far away, and the colors of surprise and passion dominate. It is to the novels of childhood, L 'odeur du cafe and Le charme des apres-midi sans fin , however, that we must turn for the special presence of color images visible in Chronique de fa derive douce to become pervasive . It seems that the closer the narrator takes us to his beginnings, to the primordial simplicity of childhood, the more these special colors take on importance. Although odors and sounds are

As the first book composed in the "tender" sequence, L 'odeur du cafe set the scene for the type of short-segmented writing typical of the series. The text is organized as a series of flashes or sensory impulses (odors, colors, tastes) around which the textual fragments crystallize. These head-centered perceptions reveal a somewhat passive but acutely aware and observant youthful witness, remarkably sensitive to impressions, and equipped with the extraordinary memory required to resurrect the scenes when as an adult he will commit them to written form. It may be noted that sounds are of lesser importance in this regard. This is a silent world: Petit-Goave is a sleepy town without much noise, where not a lot happens. In the opening pages of the novel, sensory impulses predominate. The first segment, "L 'ete 63," retraces the route leading to Petit-Goave, and as we enter the town, the "jaune feu" \[fire yellow\] (13) of the barracks building colors the scene. Da and the narrator, the principal characters of the story, and the veranda of the house , the center of the action, are then set in place . In the third segment, "Le paysage," an explicit comparison is made between what meets the narrator's eye and a typical primitive landscape, complete with the use of simple perspective in the background: "On dirait un des sin de peintre naif avec , au loin, de grosses montagnes chauves et fumantes" \[You might say a drawing by a primitive painter, with big bald and smoking mountains in the distance\] (14) . Fire ("feu," " flamme"), evocative of yellow and red, is mentioned four time s in the scene; black smoke rises to meet the "bleu clair" \[light blue\] of the sky. In segment 4, the "soleil rouge" \[red sun\] plunges into the "mer turquoise" \[turquoise sea\], framed by the coconut palms behind the aforementioned yellow barracks (15). The peasant women selling charcoal wear black dresses (15); one of them stops to urinate, emitting "un puissant jet de liquide jaune" \[a powerful spurt of yellow liquid\] (15) that the narrator duly records. Despite its formal resemblance to L 'odeur du cafe, the next novel in the chronological sequence, Le charme des apres-midi sans fin , differs from the earlier work in important ways. The writing is more narrative in character, less pictorial ; the narrator tells more stories. Predictably , the narrative segments are substantially longer. Nor is Vieux Os as sweet, innocent, and refreshingly naive as in the earlier book. He is a year older. Mortal danger proliferates in the town, and the specter of the narrator's ultimate departure from Petit-Goave rises in his consciousness. Blue skies (29) and the famous blue coffee cup (51), red bicycles (35), green flies (64), red sun (109), and yellow tractors (182-3) continue to proliferate in these pages, with the same power to color the scene and channel emotions. Vava still haunts the narrator with her yellow dress (81) and enormous, cold black eyes. But in this novel, the action leads more purposefully towards the ultimate exile of the narrator from the town, from his grandmother's nurturing influence, and from the marvels of childhood. Color erupts in the first page of the novel. The mother of the narrator's friend Rico sews multicolored dresses for sale in the market, "de jolies robes, simples et colorees" \[pretty dresses, simple and colorful\] (13). She does not hesitate to add flashes of incongruously contrasting colors to the mix: "II lui arrive aussi de faire une robe avec cinq morceaux de tissus de couleurs differentes, souvent des couleurs

\*\*\* The period of time covered by Edwidge Danticat's novel Breath, Eyes, Memory' was one of tumultuous upheaval in Haiti. More than a decade of neoliberalism overseen by Jean-Claude "Baby Doc" Duvalier had precipitated the decline of the peasant system of agriculture, causing thousands to flee rural poverty only to end up in urban slums. But despite ruthless repression, the contradictions of a society in which an enriched minority continued to flaunt its extravagancies while the majority was squeezed and battered could not be suppressed . In the late 1980s a mass movement brought down the Duvalier regime and began a process of dechoukaj - or uprooting -of the entrenched structures of power. The cult of virginity itself is located in a broader gender system that devalues women, who are responsible for domestic labor that is neither waged nor socially esteemed. In Haiti women are also traditionally responsible for the toils of petty market trade, selling food products for local markets or export crops to the speculateurs, the middlemen who deal with the merchants . This economic activity , while crucial to subsistence, is not an adequate means of support for an entire family. As Kathy McAfee explains in her study of the impact of neoliberalism on the Caribbean, women's work in the informal economy, while "essential to the sustenance of the family" is "not recognized in official production statistics.t''? While Export Processing Zones from the 1970s in Haiti as elsewhere have disproportionately employed women, the work is characterized by "sub-poverty wages and dangerous working conditions" (88) and tends to perpetuate rather than challenge women's subordinate role. Because women's productivity, while crucial, is unable to provide economic security , girl children are perceived as a burden, of less value than boy children . Even though chronic high unemployment limits male workers' earning power, when available , "men's work" such as sugar cane production, migrant agricultural and construction labor is of higher monetary value. These factors are embedded in Tante Atie's observation about the different reception of male and female children: a boy's birth is greeted with lamplight and the nightlong celebration and vigil of the father; a girl's by darkness and the mother 's loneliness (146). Yet, this particular form of state terror has its roots in Haiti's history, which has always been inextricable from global structures. As Michel-Rolph Trouillot argues, "studies \[...\] that cannot see the Duvalierist state as an outcome - albeit not an inevitable one - of that nation's historical evolution fall short of the mark" (15). Trouillot explains that Haiti 's independence after the successful revolution was from the beginning constrained by the hostility of the world's superpowers, and its developing state was characterized by the "unpredictability and instability inherent to peripheral capitalism (stemming) from dependency" (22). While throughout the nineteenth century the state was mediated and modified by the countervailing forces of civil society, the 1915-34 occupation of Haiti by the United States removed those counterwe ights and aggravated an already explosive situation in two ways. First, it heightened the economic irrationality of the system by increasing both the forced contribut ion of the peasantry to the state and the dependency on a mono crop. Second, it

Yet, suicide docs not reflect "freedom" but rather is an act of desperation indicative of the failure to survive intolerable pressures. Written at a moment when historical alternatives - so recently opened up - are again being shut down, the novel grapples with hope and despair, survival and death. Snapshots of Haiti bookend the narrative in the form of descriptions of the airport. When Sophie first leaves for the U.S.A., we hear that "(t)hey are changing the name of the airport from Francois Duvalier to Mais Gate, like it was before Francois Duvalier was president" (33); soldiers are battling student protesters, and as Sophie looks back she sees Atie, out of place in this urban world of "smiling well-dressed groups on their way to board the planes" and "jeans-clad tourists whom the panhandlers surrounded at the gate" (36). The illustration used on the cover of this book is f rom a painting by Bertelus Myrb el entitled "L 'union fait la fo rce " (2003). It is made available courtesy of Laetitia Schutt and the Haitian Arts Research Project.

About the Myrbel Painting on the Book Cover LeGrace Benson

Bertelus Myrbel' s 2003 work, L 'union fait la force (Unity makes strength), is a weave of politics, religions, history, and legend stemming directly from the artist' s participation in Haitian life today. Setting aside the charming, colorful scenes of an invented Haitian landscape so often characteristic of Haitian paintin gs, Myrbel chooses colors that are, in some places, subtle and tender and, in others, aggressively acidulen t. He draws his symbolic referenc es from the heroes of Haitian independence, from folkway s of honoring the dead, from events remembered and supposed, from Vodou and Christianity. The artist has explained certain symbol s used in his work. The large eye with the "Mission de la Paix" banner over it is the eye of God. This symbol comes into Haiti via the Masons as well as the Jesuits, and also appears in Vodou banners and paintings. The large dove beside it is the dove of peace as well as the dove of the Holy Spirit. The myriad angels hovering in the sky may look as though they have red stingers, but Myrbel tells us that these are flames of the Holy Spirit coming from their mouths . On the left is the largest of many skulls. It signifies the presence of the espri Desaline (Spirit of Dessalines) beside which is written "Moun gen yo n siprise pou nou ,. chok" (A man has a surprise for us; shock) . The string of skulls below says: "Nou tout se nennen racine" (We are all godmoth ers of the roots), an intensified way to say

532

Benson

that "We are your forebears, your ancestors." Each wears a blue and red headband, and the topmost one bears two banners, one the original blue and red flag of Dessalines, the other the black and red of his later battle flag. The large helmet with USA inscribed on it represents the US with its arms and army. Beneath it is a dark place, signed as "du lamo," that is, "of death." Below are huge bones, also bound in red and blue, out of which pour streams of water. These are the dry bones of the revolution that magically refresh the streams with living water. Rays from the eye of God descend to the bones, enabling them to give the water. On the bones is written, "Se Kou pou nou tout" (It is a blow to us all). Water from the bones pours into the stream, on either side of which are traditional candle and ribbon offerings as prayers for peace. In the stream the flowers bloom with the red and blue of Haiti's flag over them. On some rocks is written drapo bikolo (the two colored Haitian flag - bicolor in contrast to the French tricolor or the U.S. red, white and blue), and below that the motto from the flag, "L 'union fait la force" (Unity makes strength). Above the stream on the right is an eye peering out of a dark rock. A sign points to it, "Licife" (Lucifer) . Above that some ordinary angels without the fires of the spirit hover over the skulls of some "Boko cimitie" (Bokor of the cemetery) who are evildoers. Their banners are all red, indicating aggressive Petro spirits. A jar containing spirits and three more skulls with Haitian colors lie beside a cross and an electricity pole. Bead strings and colored scarves are on the cross and standards with colored banners lie on the ground nearby. These call upon various Vodou lwa (spirits) to come into the community to help them win the peace. Mrybel explained that there is an electricity pole beside the cross because we live in modem times. Electricity is what brings us most of our messages, so the message of peace needs the telephone and light pole to come to the people. This visual poem brings you the artist's message of hope. Bertelus Myrbel , a young artist from Milot and Cap Haitien, has studied in Port-au-Prince and with the artists of the extended circle of the late Philome Obin in Cap Haitien. His works are in collections in Haiti, the United States, Germany and France, and have been featured in group exhibitions throughout the United States.

Addre ssed co all readers of Our Nig, from professional scholars of African American writing through co a more general readership, th is book explores both Our Nil's key cultural contexts and its historical and literary significance as a narrative. Harriet E. Wilson's Our Nig (1859) is a startling tale of the mistreatment of a young African American mulatto woman, Frado, living in New England at a time when slavery, though abolished in the North, still existed in the South. Frado, a Northern 'free black', yet treated as badly as many Southern slaves of the time, is unforgettably portrayed as experiencing and resisting vicious mistreatment. To achieve th is d isturbing portrait, Harriet Wilson's book combines several different literary genres - realist novel, autobiography, abolitionist slave narrative and sentimental fiction . R.\]. Ellis explores the relationship of Our Nig to these genres and, additionally, co laboring class writing (Harriet Wilson was an indentured farm servant) . He identifies the way Our Nig stands as a double first: the first separately-published novel written in English by an African American female it is also one of the first by a member of the laboring class about the laboring class. This study explores how, as a result, Our Nig tells a series of disturbing two-stories about America 's con stitutional guarantee of 'freedom' and the way these relate co Frado's farm life.

When did the intimate dialogue between Africa, Europe, and the Americas begin? Looking back, it seems as if these three continents have always been each other 's significant others . Europe created its own modem identity by using Africa as a mirror, but Africans traveled to Europe and America long before the European age of discovery , and African culture s can be said to lie at the root of European culture . This intertwining has become ever more visible : Nowadays Africa emerge s as a highly visible presence in the Americas, and African American styles capture Europe 's youth, many of whom are of (North-) African descent. This entanglement, however , remains both productive and destructive. The continental econom ies are intertwined in ways disastrous for Africa, and African knowledge is all too often exported and translated for US and European scholarly aims, which increases the intercontinental knowledge gap. T he present collection of essays by renowned writers and scholars addresses these issues and helps to ground the ongoing debate about the African diaspora in a more solid theoretical framework. [1](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa1)_In 2019, your inaugural lecture at the Collège de France, “Urgence(s) d’écrire, rêve(s) d’habiter” \[Pressure(s) to write, dream(s) of dwelling\], underscored the ties between Haitian literature and history. You brought the lecture to a close by speaking about the specificity of poetry and literature written by women. This interview by correspondence will focus primarily on these two points._

[2](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa2)**Clara Palmiste & Michelle Zancarini-Fournel**: _Current thinking often affirms that literature makes it possible to talk about times, conjunctures and configurations that historical accounts sometimes struggle to capture. We’d like to consider three key moments in the history of Haiti, examining how writers have depicted them in works of fiction and poetry: the 1803-1804 turning point in the revolution that paved the way for the world’s first Black republic, the American occupation (1915-1934), and the dictatorship in the late twentieth century. You have described the literature of exile elsewhere; could you explain how the writers who remained in Haiti have written about these difficult moments?_

[3](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa3)**Yanick Lahens**: The prelude to 1804, the period of slavery, is hardly ever mentioned in Haitian literature, as if independence completely erased it. However, nothing could be further from the truth. The scars remain. Until very recently, history books showcased the political battles of heroes. The first Haitian novel, _Stella_, written by Emeryc Bergeaud and published in 1859, [\[1\]](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#no1) provides a cursory account of the battle for Independence, only skims over the time of slavery and colonization, and concentrates rather on the rivalry between the black leader Toussaint Louverture and the mixed-descent leader André Rigaud, with a view to criticizing colorism. [\[2\]](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#no2) And yet, we know that in the Caribbean, especially in the English-speaking Caribbean, the theme of the Middle Passage is ever-present.

[4](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa4)Marie Chauvet \[also known as Vieux-Chauvet\] was the first to depict colonization in La _Danse sur le volcan_ (1957), which is set in the theater world and recounts the life of an actress of color. Though colonization serves as the backdrop and we feel the initial stirrings which will lead to liberation, slavery as such is not really depicted. It’s not until Évelyne Trouillot’s _Rosalie l’infâme_ (2003) that slavery, the conditions of slaves, and the memory of the Middle Passage serve as the framework for a novel.

[5](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa5)As for the periods of American occupation and the Duvalier dictatorship, I revisit them in _Bain de lune_ (2014), in the small rural village of Anse-Bleue – the entire Haitian twentieth century begins with that occupation. The novel ends with \[J.-B.\] Aristide’s coming to power, which in a way brings the twentieth century to a close, after dealing with the Duvalier era, of course. The personal and the historical become intertwined from the point of view and in the voice of the farmers of the village, and not of city dwellers. Marie Chauvet’s rendering of the Duvalier era in _Amour Colère Folie_ (1968) is superb, as are Kettly Mars’s _Saisons sauvages_ (2010), Marie Célie Agnant’s _Le livre d_’_Emma_ (2004) and _Un alligator nommé Rosa_ (2008), and Évelyne Trouillot’s _La Mémoire aux abois_ (2010). Two women tackled in writing the US Occupation while it was underway. However, one of them – Cléante Valcin \[publishing as Mme Virgile Valcin\] in _La Blanche Négresse_ (1934) – deals only briefly with the colorism that the occupiers exacerbated, while the other – Annie Desroy in _Le Joug_ (1934) – focuses more on the ordeal caused by the occupation for the bourgeoisie of the time.

[6](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa6)Some women writers, such as Marie Chauvet and Jeanine Tavernier Louis went into exile, while others, such as Marie-Thérèse Colimon Hall and Paulette Poujol Oriol, continued to live under the dictatorship. Yanick Jean came back out of exile and wrote a magnificent collection of poems, _La Fidélité non plus…_ (2003)

[7](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa7)**CP & MZF** : _Does the representation of emblematic female figures (like Nerline, a women’s rights activist, in your own novel_ Douces déroutes, _come from a desire to shed light on forgotten periods of history, on women’s struggles?_

[8](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa8)**Yanick Lahens** : It was more of a nod to the struggle of the young women in Haiti today, those who are taking up the torch carried by groundbreakers of the past such as Sanite Belair, a fighter in the Indigenous Army \[of the 1804 Revolution\], who was the spouse of an officer in that same army; Toya, and other women who were active in the same struggle for independence; then in the early twentieth century, the Sylvain sisters. Suzanne was the first woman, alongside Jean Prince Mars, to take up field research and to compile the texts of oral literature, while her sister Jeanne was Haiti’s first female doctor in the same period. And let’s not forget the women of the _Ligue d’Action feminine sociale_ \[Women’s League for Social Action\] who overtly championed women’s causes as early as the late 1930s. The league had a long lifespan and one of its members, the journalist Yvonne Hakim Rimpel, was arrested and tortured under the Duvalier dictatorship.

[9](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa9)Today, it’s excellent that women’s stories are coming out of the shadows. More than half of humanity (we make up over 50%) is starting to make its voice heard.

[10](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa10)Young women like Nerline in _Douces déroutes_ are on the front lines of activism against corruption today, both out on the streets and on social media, and they are demanding accountability. They are visible and have a voice.

[11](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa11)**CP & MZF**: _There is much discussion of so-called “littérature féminine” in the French-speaking West Indies: Maryse Condé is well known, but apart from your name, other women writers from Haiti are rarely referenced. Could you introduce us to your literary pantheon and tell us which authors are writing today? In what language(s) do they write?_

[12](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa12)**Yanick Lahens** : There are well-known authors like Évelyne Trouillot, Kettly Mars, Marie Alice Théard, and Emmelie Prophète. The new generation includes Martine Fidèle, Sybille Claude, Milady Auguste and Saika Céus, who wrote the novel _Tifi_ in Creole, following in the footsteps of Mercédès Foucard Guignard, also known as Deita, who published _Esperans Dezire_ in 1989. An entire host of young women poets write in both languages. I was very recently delighted to discover some of them on the Plimay website. [\[3\]](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#no3)

[13](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa13)But I would also include novelists like Edwidge Danticat, who writes in English, and Micheline Dusseck, who writes in Spanish, under the banner of this national literature, because it seems to me that literature has to engage in a new configuring of the world that calls on us to discard nineteenth-century criteria for nationhood. There is Haitian literature in English and in Spanish. Some young people leave to study in the Dominican Republic and take part in literary circles there. Jean-Jacques Pierre-Paul, a doctor by profession and one of the young poets in the public eye in Chile, is another such case. Migration compels us to rethink notions like nations and languages in different ways. Languages are no longer bound to a single flag, nor to a single homeland.

[14](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa14)Better still, women were in fact the first to write in two languages other than those spoken in their home country. This leads us to look with new light at how the notion of identity was defined in their original, patriarchal culture.

[15](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa15)**CP & MZF**: _Would you speak about Haiti as having women’s literature, feminine literature, and feminist literature? How would you classify authors? Have they formed groups or remained separate individuals?_

[16](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa16)**Yanick Lahens**: Literature is not gendered. I’ve maintained that for years. Sitting at the blank page or screen, we experience the anxiety or the joy of writing the same as male writers do. But that absolutely doesn’t erase our situatedness. Patriarchal societies have boxed us into roles and into a position. This remains true, even if the matriarchy created by history and by slavery in the French West Indies compels us to address this particular patriarchy in all its specificity and with all its nuances. And here, I’m speaking for Haiti, the place I know best.

[17](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa17)This is among one of the many reasons that I prefer talking about the women in Haitian society. When we talk about the social make-up of Haiti, we must never lose sight of the fact that the majority of a population of over 24 ethnic groups built a civilization opposed to the plantation system by creating a language, a religion, a code of law different from the Napoleonic Code, marital relationships, a way of occupying space, and so on and so forth. They put an undeniable distance between themselves and the new masters of the country, the Creoles, who in the aftermath of 1804 sought to reproduce the former colonial model, which would prevail in the Caribbean and Latin America for many years to come.

[18](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa18)Until very recently, women who wrote books belonged to the Westernized bourgeois classes or to the middle classes, so the positions they defended belonged to a liberation fashioned after Simone de Beauvoir or Kate Millett, and they wrote in French. Rural working-class women didn’t write, but held spaces of power, such as in the Voodoo religion, which afforded them equal footing with men in priesthood. So for instance, in her book _Nan dòmi_ (2013), Mimerose Beaubrun, lead singer of the music group Boukman Eksperyans, recounts her initiation into Voodoo by a priestess. Furthermore, rural women also bridged the gap between the countryside and the city because they were the ones who travelled to sell produce in urban markets. Their words unquestionably carried a certain power linked to these social and economic functions. With accelerated urbanization, a new group of women came to make up the urban working classes; these women were the heads of single-parent households and were able to raise their children in large part thanks to informal trade, since the vast majority of men within such areas were faced with unemployment. In my novel _La Couleur de l’aube_, Angélique and Joyeuse belong to this category and live in one of these families. The children and grandchildren of these women are the men and women who are writing today. And unlike the women writers of my generation, such as Évelyne Trouillot or Kettly Mars, they went through schools in which Creole had its place and lived their childhoods in a time when Creole had status as an official language and had become the dominant language in broadcast media. We also mustn’t forget the colossal work accomplished by feminist organizations for women’s equality. The transformation is absolutely thrilling.

[19](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa19)**CP & MZF**: _Do female authors have status, a place within the community of “gens de lettres” \[recognized writers\]?_

[20](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa20)**Yanick Lahens**: For women, writing means laying oneself bare because women’s first clothing is supposed to be silence and self-effacement. Writing means undressing and moving into a forbidden territory. We, the women writers of Haiti today, have our place in society; we’ve got recognition. However, we’re constantly confronted with the same questions: _“Why are there so many female characters in your novels?”_ I’ve never heard anyone ask a man a question in that way: _“Why are there so many male characters in your novels?”_ Men have been speaking and writing in Haitian literature for over 200 years. These kinds of questions act as a barometer of the immense transgression (against history, against society) that women commit when they dare to speak or write. We’ve only just begun, and people are going to have to get used to hearing us from now on.

[21](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa21)I would say that we can talk about “feminine literature” any time we put the veil of silence or effacement back on, and so write only what others expect us to write. Any time that is, that we fall back into the trap of stereotypes. We may never be able to escape completely from this, and we will sometimes be the _bad feminists_ that Roxane Gay humorously portrays. We are feminists every time we remove that all too restrictive garment, ignore the walls erected about us, and dare to speak freely. So we inevitably oscillate between the two.

[22](https://shs.cairn.info/journal-clio-women-gender-history-2019-2-page-241?lang=en#pa22)And above all, we must avoid any trap that confines us. The human condition is vast in the infinitely small, just as it is in the infinitely great, and we mustn’t relinquish any part of this human condition.

Bibliography
------------

*   Agnant, Marie Célie. 2004. _Le Livre d’Emma_. La Roque d’Anthéron: Éditions Vents d’ailleurs. \[Translated by Zilpha Ellis as _The Book of Emma_. Ontario: Insomniac Press, 2006\].
*   Agnant, Marie Célie. 2008. _Un alligator nommé Rosa_. Montreal: Éditions du Remue-Ménage.
*   Beaubrun, Mimerose. 2010. _Nan dòmi_. La Roque d’Anthéron: Éditions Vents d’ailleurs. \[Translated by D.J. Walker as _Nan domi: an initiate’s journey into Haitian Voodoo_. San Francisco: City Lights Books, 2013\].
*   Bergeaud, Emeryc. 1859. _Stella._ Paris: É. Dentu, Libraire-éditeur. \[Translated by Lesley S. Curtis & Christen Mucher as _Stella: A Novel of the Haitian Revolution._ New York and London: NYU Press, 2015\].
*   Desroy, Annie. 1934. _Le Joug._ Port-au-Prince: Imp. Modèle.
*   Jean, Yanick. 2003 \[1st edn Port-au-Prince, Haïti, 1988\]. _La Fidélité non plus._ Montreal: Mémoire d’encrier.
*   Céus, Saika. 2017. _Tifi_. Port-au-Prince: Henri Deschamps.
*   Foucard Gugnard, Mercédès. 1989. _Esperans Désiré_. Port-au-Prince: Deschamps.
*   Gay, Roxane. 2014. _Bad Feminist_. New York: Harper Perennial.
*   Lahens, Yanick. 2008. _La Couleur de l’aube._ Paris: Sabine Wespieser. \[Translated by Allison Layland as _The Colour of Dawn_. Bridgend, Wales: Seren Books, 2013\].
*   Lahens, Yanick. 2014. _Bain de lune._ Paris: Sabine Wespieser. \[Translated by Emily Gogolak as _Moonbath_. Dallas, TX: Deep Vellum, 2017\].
*   Lahens, Yanick. 2018. _Douces déroutes_. Paris: Sabine Wespieser.
*   Mars, Kettly. 2010. _Saisons sauvages_. Paris: Mercure de France. \[Translated by Jeanine Herman as _Savage Seasons_. Lincoln and London: University of Nebraska Press, 2015\].
*   Ndiaye, Christiane, 2009, _Stella_ d’Émeric Bergeaud : une écriture épique de l’histoire. _Itinéraires_ 2: 19-31.
*   Trouillot, Évelyne. 2003. _Rosalie l’infâme._ Paris: Éditions Dapper. \[Translated by M.A. Salvadon as _The Infamous Rosalie._ Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 2013\].
*   Trouillot, Évelyne. 2010. _La Mémoire aux abois_. Paris: Éditions Hoëbeke. \[Translated by Paul Curtis Daw as _Memory at Bay_. Charlottesville: University of Virginia Press, 2015\].
*   Valcin, Cléante \[Mme Virgile Valcin\] 1934. _La Blanche négresse._ Port-au-Prince: Presses d’Haïti.
*   Vieux\-Chauvet, Marie. 1957. _La Danse sur le volcan._ Paris: Plon. \[Translated by Kaiama L. Gover as _A Dance on the Volcano_. Brooklyn, NY: First Archipelago Books, 2017\].
*   Vieux\-Chauvet, Marie. 1968. _Amour Colère Folie._ Paris: Blanche Gallimard. \[Paperback edition, Paris: Zulma, 2015; translated by Rose-Myriam Rejouis & Val Vinokur as _Love, Anger, Madness: a Haitian triptych_. New York: Modern Library 2009\].
